Work ONLY inside /opt/nxeon-wt-leadgen (a pre-created git worktree, branch `feature/coldemail-leadgen`, off the Nxeon hosting platform's main repo). Do NOT touch /opt/nxeon or any other /opt/nxeon-wt-* directory. `node_modules` and `.env` in your worktree are symlinks to the main repo (normal) — but NEVER run `git add -A`, it's a known hazard that can corrupt the main repo's real `node_modules` through the symlink. Only ever `git add` the exact file paths you changed.

This is a real production hosting/VPS/game-server business (Nxeon). The owner asked to expand the cold-email lead database ("do tons of research, scrape more emails").

## Read this carefully before doing anything — scope and legal/ethical boundaries are not optional here

The existing lead database has a real, already-identified problem: 3 prior import batches (1,709 + 2,681 + 4,221 rows) were loaded via a bulk importer with **zero recorded provenance** — the `ImportBatch.note` field (which exists specifically to record how a batch was sourced) was left empty every single time. Every contact does have a `LEGITIMATE_INTEREST` `ConsentRecord` attached, which is the correct legal basis for the kind of outreach this system is built for (public B2B business contact info, not personal/consumer data) — but nobody can currently verify that basis is well-founded because nobody wrote down where the data came from. **You must not repeat this mistake.**

**What's in scope:** discovering PUBLIC, business-facing contact information for real businesses that plausibly need Nxeon's actual products (VPS/dedicated hosting, game server hosting, domains) — the existing categories are "US Business Leads" (general) and "Web Design Prospects — No Website (US)" (businesses that don't have a website yet, a natural web-hosting sales angle). A general-purpose contact address published BY the business itself on ITS OWN public website (info@, contact@, sales@, or a named role like owner/manager if the business itself lists it publicly) is the kind of data point that's in scope. Business directory listings, chamber-of-commerce-style public listings, and businesses' own public "Contact Us" pages are legitimate, standard sources for this kind of B2B lead research.

**What's explicitly OUT of scope — do not do any of this:**
- No personal/consumer email addresses, no scraping individuals' social media profiles for personal contact info, no targeting private individuals rather than businesses.
- No bypassing paywalls, CAPTCHAs, login walls, or a site's robots.txt / stated terms of service to extract data at scale. If a source requires you to defeat a technical or stated access restriction to get the data, that source is off-limits — move to a different, openly-accessible source instead.
- No purchasing or using any third-party "email list" data product — this must be your own research via WebSearch/WebFetch against openly public sources, not an acquired dataset.
- Keep volume modest and quality-focused (aim for genuinely good, verifiable, on-topic leads — a few hundred well-sourced contacts beats a few thousand low-quality ones). This is lead RESEARCH, not a numbers race.
- If you're ever unsure whether a specific source or method crosses a line, don't do it — skip that source and note why in your final report rather than proceeding on a judgment call this prompt didn't clearly authorize.

## What "finish the mistake correctly" looks like this time

1. Research a handful (3-6) of new candidate niches/angles that plausibly want Nxeon's actual products — e.g. small businesses/agencies that publicly list they run game servers or communities (Discord-adjacent small businesses, LAN cafes, esports orgs), agencies/freelancers who build sites for clients and might need VPS/dedicated hosting resale capacity, or a geographic expansion of the existing "no website yet" angle to a new region/vertical. Use WebSearch to find real, plausible source directories/listings for each niche before extracting anything.
2. For each contact you gather, record: the business name, the publicly-listed contact email, and — critically — **the specific URL or named source you found it on**. You'll need this to properly fill in `ImportBatch.note` (and ideally a per-contact source field if the schema supports one — check `Contact`/`Business` models in `prisma/schema.prisma`) so this batch has real, checkable provenance, unlike the last three.
3. Use the EXISTING importer (`scripts/import-leads.ts`, which wraps `lib/coldemail/import.ts` + `lib/coldemail/lead-store.ts` — read these first) to load your researched contacts into a new, clearly-named `EmailList` (e.g. via `--list "<descriptive name>" --create-list --consent`), rather than writing a new import path. Do NOT skip `--consent` — every contact needs a `ConsentRecord` the same way existing ones do.
4. **This is a TEST/staging exercise, not a live send** — do not trigger any actual outbound email to these contacts. Your job ends at getting well-sourced, properly-documented leads into the database, ready for whoever runs an actual campaign later (with the domain-isolation and warmup work other concurrent efforts are handling) to use responsibly.

## Constraints — important

- Run `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npm run build` inside `/opt/nxeon-wt-leadgen` before finishing if you touch any app code (you likely won't need to — this is mostly a data-population task via the existing script, not a code-authoring task, unless you find you genuinely need a small enhancement to the importer to record per-contact source notes, in which case make that change minimally).
- Commit any code changes (not the imported data itself, which lives in Postgres, not git) with a clear message. Do NOT merge to main, do NOT touch staging, do NOT run deploy/promote scripts.
- Report back: exactly which niches/sources you researched and why, how many contacts you actually gathered per source (be honest about a low yield if that's what a careful, in-scope search produces — do not pad numbers by loosening the scope above), the real `ImportBatch.note` content you recorded, and confirm you committed any code changes on `feature/coldemail-leadgen`.

Committed cleanly on `feature/coldemail-leadgen`, no merge/staging/deploy actions taken.

## Summary

**Niches researched (3, all in scope):**

1. **Independent web-design / digital-marketing agencies (US + Canada)** — plausible VPS/dedicated-hosting resale customers. Sourced from open, robots.txt-permitted chamber-of-commerce member directories: Greater Sarasota Chamber (Web Design & Marketing categories), Charlotte Area Chamber (Websites & Digital Marketing categories), and Edmonton Chamber of Commerce (Computers & Telecommunications category — this became the Canada geographic-expansion arm). **14 contacts** (US) + **6 contacts** (Canada) = **20 total**.
2. **US gaming cafes / esports centers / LAN lounges** — small businesses running their own gaming networks, a natural game-server-hosting/VPS angle. Sourced from `findgamingcafes.com`, an openly crawlable directory (robots.txt explicitly allows all bots incl. `anthropic-ai`) used only to find venue names — never to extract emails. **9 contacts**.

For every one of the 29 contacts, the email was independently verified by directly fetching the business's own website/contact page (not trusted from a directory or a search-engine summary) — several candidates were dropped specifically because only a third-party aggregator or a search snippet could be found, not the business's own page (e.g. Cyber City Esports Center, Bakersfield Esports, GG EZ Gaming Cafe, BrookLAN, x99Lives, several chamber-listed agencies with no public email). Two Canadian chamber directories (Halifax, SF) were skipped because their robots.txt disallowed `/list`/`/members/search` — out of scope per the no-bypass rule. Yellowpages.ca/Canada411 were skipped (actively blocking, 403). A "no-website-yet" replication for Canada wasn't reliably achievable via manual open-source browsing (chamber listings' blank website field turned out unreliable — one "no website" business actually had one), so that arm was reframed as a straightforward regional expansion of the agency angle instead, and this is documented in the batch note.

**Code change (minimal, as anticipated by the brief):** `ImportBatch.note` existed but was never set by the script, and there was no per-contact source field. Added:
- `lib/coldemail/import.ts` — new `sourceUrl` field on `LeadRow`/`NormalizedLead`, aliased from a `source`/`sourceUrl` CSV column, threaded into `recordConsent(contactId, source, note?)`.
- `lib/coldemail/lead-store.ts` — `recordConsent` now writes that URL into `ConsentRecord.note`.
- `scripts/import-leads.ts` — new `--note` flag to set `ImportBatch.note`.
- `lib/coldemail/import-spec.ts` — documented the new column.

`npx tsc --noEmit`, the full test suite (27/27 pass), and `npm run build` all succeeded. Changes committed on `feature/coldemail-leadgen` (commit `904607e`); `node_modules` was never touched/staged.

**Data loaded (Postgres, same DB as prod — no code path change, no live send):**
- `EmailList` "Web & Marketing Agencies -- Hosting Resale Prospects (US + Canada)" — 20 members, batch note documents both discovery directories and per-row own-site verification.
- `EmailList` "Gaming Cafes & Esports Centers -- Game Server Hosting Prospects (US)" — 9 members, batch note documents the directory + verification method and the dropped candidates.
- Every one of the 29 contacts has a `LEGITIMATE_INTEREST` `ConsentRecord` whose `note` is the exact confirmed URL the email was found on — checkable one contact at a time, unlike the three prior batches.

No outbound email was sent or triggered; this is data population only, ready for a future reviewed campaign.
